extracted.intended_audience: high-school and introductory college students studying international public relations (AP/intro PR learners)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate Grunig & Hunt's four models of public relations (press agentry/publicity, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric) and their application in international and digital contexts. The guide explains characteristics, ethical implications, examples, and limits of each model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agentry/publicity model
rubrics_metrics.description: Oldest and most basic model in Grunig's theory; focuses on generating publicity and attention for clients or organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizes media coverage and public attention above all else; uses persuasive techniques such as exaggeration, hype, or selective information sharing. Measures success primarily by amount of media coverage or publicity generated. Operates as a one-way communication approach (information flows from organization to public without feedback). Typical examples: celebrity publicists, movie studios creating buzz, political campaigns using soundbites, product launches with promotional stunts. Ethical concerns: potential deception and lack of strategic depth; can misalign organizational goals with public expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public information model
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolved in response to criticism of press agentry; emphasizes truthful and accurate information dissemination to inform rather than persuade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizes accuracy and completeness; relies on journalistic principles of fact-checking and objectivity to build credibility and trust. Primarily one-way but may include limited feedback mechanisms; common tools include press releases, fact sheets, annual reports, informational websites. Typical users: government agencies, nonprofits, educational institutions, public safety organizations during emergencies. Measures of effectiveness focus on credibility and reliability rather than sheer publicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way asymmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporates feedback and research to improve message effectiveness while still aiming to persuade audiences to meet organizational goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses audience research and behavioral science (message testing, focus groups, A/B testing, segmentation) to craft persuasive messages. Gathers feedback via surveys, social media monitoring, and analytics to refine communications. Prioritizes organizational objectives over mutual benefit, raising ethical questions about manipulation and power imbalances. Often used in corporate PR, advertising, and targeted marketing communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way symmetric model
rubrics_metrics.description: Considered by Grunig to be the most ethical and effective model; focuses on mutual understanding, dialogue, negotiation, and relationship-building between organizations and publics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages open, honest communication and active listening to find shared interests and win-win outcomes. Measures success by quality of relationships and mutual satisfaction rather than only by persuasion metrics. Implementation challenges include resource intensity, need for organizational commitment, cultural/political resistance, high transparency demands, and difficulty quantifying relational outcomes. Requires willingness to adapt organizational policies and accept changes in both parties' attitudes/behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-way vs two-way communication (comparative criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes models by directionality of communication: one-way models disseminate information, two-way models incorporate feedback and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-way (press agentry, public information) is appropriate for quick information dissemination or when audiences are expected to be passive; two-way (asymmetric, symmetric) supports engagement and long-term relationship building. One-way may be useful in crisis situations where rapid dissemination is critical; two-way is generally better for trust and sustained stakeholder relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymmetric vs symmetric approaches (comparative criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasts approaches that prioritize organizational goals (asymmetric) with those seeking balance and mutual benefit (symmetric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asymmetric approaches may generate short-term gains through targeted persuasion but risk damaging trust and causing ethical issues. Symmetric approaches aim for balanced outcomes that satisfy both organizations and publics and build stronger, more resilient relationships over time, though they require more investment and openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical implications of each model
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates models on ethical grounds: press agentry raises manipulation concerns; public information improves ethics but lacks engagement; two-way asymmetric can be manipulative despite research use; two-way symmetric is most ethical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key ethical considerations include transparency, truthfulness, manipulation, power dynamics, and whether communication seeks mutual benefit. Practitioners must weigh short-term persuasive gains against long-term trust and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application in international PR (cultural adaptation criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assesses how suitable each model is across cultures and contexts; models must be adapted to local norms, values, and power structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Press agentry may be more accepted in cultures with different ethical norms; public information aligns with cultures valuing authority/hierarchy; two-way models may face challenges in high-context or collectivist cultures where direct dialogue or confrontation is less common. Global strategies often mix models and require balancing global brand consistency with local relevance. Case examples: U.S. political campaigns (press agentry/asymmetric), EU institutions (public information), Japanese firms (consensus-based symmetric tendencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance in the digital age / social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers how digital platforms change the application and effectiveness of Grunig's models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media enables real-time two-way dialogue and social listening, blurs lines between organizations and publics (user-generated content), and creates new forms of press agentry (viral content, influencer partnerships). Two-way symmetric approaches can thrive in online communities; two-way asymmetric uses big data and targeted ads; public information expands through online newsrooms. Practitioners should adapt tactics (monitoring, engagement, analytics) while being mindful of platform dynamics and ethical privacy concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints on implementing models
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies real-world barriers that affect which model an organization can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constraints include limited resources, organizational culture and leadership resistance, legal and regulatory restrictions, and time pressures (e.g., crises requiring fast, one-way messaging). These factors may prevent full implementation of the ideal (symmetric) model and necessitate trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures of success and evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Different models imply different success metrics: media coverage for press agentry; credibility/truthfulness for public information; persuasion effectiveness for asymmetric; relationship quality for symmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should choose metrics aligned to their model and goals: quantity of coverage, sentiment analysis, engagement/relationship indicators, and long-term trust. Two-way symmetric outcomes are often harder to quantify with traditional PR metrics, requiring relational and qualitative evaluation tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiques, limitations, and alternative theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges scholarly critiques of Grunig's models and points to complementary or competing theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations include gaps between theory and practice, cultural variability, and evolving media/technology contexts. Alternatives and extensions: Excellence Theory (organizational factors), Relationship Management Theory (long-term stakeholder relationships), Situational Theory of Publics (when publics become active), and critical theories that interrogate power dynamics. Ongoing research refines and expands these frameworks.
